summary: Joseph of Arimathea asks Pilate for Jesus’ body and, with Nicodemus, wraps it in linen and spices and lays it in a new tomb as the women watch.
key_insight: John calls Joseph a disciple “secretly, for fear of the Jews.” Mark says he went to Pilate “taking courage.” The cross scattered the Twelve, but it brought two hidden followers, both leading men in Jerusalem, into the open.
story: Evening was coming on. It was the Preparation Day, the day before the Sabbath. {Mk} Joseph of Arimathea was a rich man {Mt} and a prominent member of the council. {Mk} He was a good and just man who had not consented to the council’s decision and deed, and he was waiting for the kingdom of God. {Lk} He was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews. {Jn}

Taking courage, Joseph went in to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Pilate marveled that He was already dead. He summoned the centurion and asked whether Jesus had been dead for some time, and when he learned it from the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph. {Mk}

Joseph bought fine linen and took the body down. {Mk} Nicodemus, who had first come to Jesus by night, came as well, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. Together they bound the body of Jesus in strips of linen with the spices, “as the custom of the Jews is to bury.” {Jn}

In the place where Jesus was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. {Jn} It was Joseph’s own tomb, which he had cut out of the rock. {Mt} Because it was the Preparation Day and the tomb was nearby, they laid Jesus there. {Jn} Joseph rolled a large stone against the door of the tomb and went away. {Mt}

Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb. {Mt} The women who had come with Jesus from Galilee saw the tomb and how His body was laid. Then they went home and prepared spices and fragrant oils, and they rested on the Sabbath according to the commandment. {Lk}
differences: Matthew calls Joseph a rich man and a disciple; Mark, a prominent council member who took courage; Luke, a good and just man who had not consented to the council’s decision; John, a disciple in secret for fear of the Jews.
Only Mark tells that Pilate marveled that Jesus was already dead and checked with the centurion.
Only John tells of Nicodemus, the hundred pounds of spices and the garden.
Only Matthew says the tomb was Joseph’s own, cut by him from the rock. Matthew and Mark name the two Marys; Luke alone says the women prepared spices and rested on the Sabbath.

fit.question: John says Joseph and Nicodemus bound Jesus’ body with about a hundred pounds of spices. Yet Luke says the women went home and prepared spices, and Mark says they bought spices after the Sabbath (Mark 16:1). Why more spices, and when were they made ready?

points.label: A hurried burial
points.text: Jesus died about three in the afternoon, and the Sabbath began at sunset. In a few hours Joseph had to see Pilate, buy linen, take the body down and lay it in the tomb. The men did what they could in the time they had; the women’s return shows they did not think the burial complete.

points.label: The women’s own gift
points.text: The women had watched from opposite the tomb. Anointing the body was an act of love they wanted to give with their own hands, whatever the men had done.

points.label: Friday and Saturday evening
points.text: Luke says they prepared spices and oils before the Sabbath began. Mark says that when the Sabbath was past, after sunset on Saturday, they bought spices. Both fit: they began on Friday and bought more when the Sabbath ended.

fit.note: The details fit a burial done in haste before sunset and meant to be finished in love afterward. Nothing here requires an error.
fit.short: The men’s burial was hurried before sunset; the women prepared spices Friday, bought more Saturday evening, and came to finish it.

scene.label: Before sunset
scene.text: The law said a hanged man’s body “shall not remain overnight on the tree” (Deuteronomy 21:23), and the Sabbath began at sunset. Romans often left the bodies of the crucified unburied; Joseph’s request spared Jesus that.

scene.label: Arimathea
scene.text: Luke calls it “a city of the Jews.” Its location is uncertain. Many identify it with Ramathaim, the hometown of Samuel’s family (1 Samuel 1:1), northwest of Jerusalem.

scene.label: A rock tomb
scene.text: Wealthy families cut tombs into the limestone hillsides around Jerusalem, with a low entrance and a ledge or niche inside for the body. A heavy stone closed the door; the Gospels say this one was rolled into place.

scene.label: A hundred pounds
scene.text: The Roman pound was about three-quarters of ours, so Nicodemus brought about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes. It was a burial fit for a king; when King Asa died, he was laid in a bed “filled with spices” (2 Chronicles 16:14).

scene.label: With the rich
scene.text: Isaiah said the Servant’s grave would be made “with the wicked,” and “with the rich at His death” (Isaiah 53:9). Jesus was crucified between criminals and buried in a rich man’s tomb.

witnesses.matthew: Matthew says Joseph was rich and laid Jesus in “his new tomb,” details that fit Isaiah 53:9. He ends with Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sitting opposite the tomb, the witnesses who will come back on the first day of the week.
witnesses.mark: Mark records that Pilate checked with the centurion before releasing the body, so Rome’s own officer confirmed that Jesus was dead. Mark also notes that the women saw where He was laid; those who later find the tomb empty knew which tomb it was.
witnesses.luke: Luke stresses Joseph’s character: “a good and just man” who had not agreed with the council. He alone tells that the women prepared spices and then rested on the Sabbath “according to the commandment,” faithful even in grief.
witnesses.john: John alone brings back Nicodemus, who came to Jesus by night (3:2) and later spoke up for Him in the council (7:50–51). John records the garden, the new tomb and the spices bound in with the linen, and he notes that the nearness of the tomb decided where Jesus was laid.

seeing.reveals: Jesus truly died, as a Roman officer confirmed, and was truly buried. Even in death His body was treated with honor, and the Scriptures about Him held true, down to a rich man’s tomb.
seeing.living: Joseph and Nicodemus came forward when there seemed to be nothing left to gain and much to lose. Love for Jesus that has stayed hidden can still step into the open. Ask where you have kept your faith quiet out of fear, and what honoring Jesus openly would look like there.
seeing.ponder: Where have you followed Jesus secretly, and what would it mean to take courage as Joseph did?

preaching.big_idea: The cross brought secret disciples into the open, and they buried Jesus with honor.
outline: A body laid in the rock (46)
preaching.watch_for: Mark lines up witnesses: the centurion confirms the death (vv. 44–45), and the women note the tomb (v. 47). The same women come back to that tomb in 16:1–4.
